units.text: In the archives of St Andrews University in Scotland, an ancient leather tome from 1578 holds a drawing of a towering, skeletal man with bulging forehead veins and sunken dark eyes.
His name was Herbert Solomon, and the town that feared him made a fatal mistake.
In the winter of 1577, children began vanishing from the isolated village of Ettrick.
First little Alana by an old stone well, then nine more children torn from the freezing cobblestone streets.
Terrified parents turned their suspicion toward an outsider living deep in the woods: Herbert Solomon.
Ravaged by an emaciated wasting sickness, Solomon lived in a secluded cabin, carving beautiful wooden dolls and leaving them on tree stumps for the local children.
But fear blinded the townsfolk.
A mob marched into the pines, barred his cabin, and burned him alive.
Yet the disappearances did not stop.
A dense fog swallowed Ettrick, and Solomon's tall, shadowy phantom began stalking the courtyards at night.
Snatched from her bed, another girl vanished.
Even inside the stone church, his tall form flickered behind the pillars.
Desperate, the local vicar and armed men ambushed the figure in the street with torches and holy water.
Trapped and burning, the gaunt spirit darted into an open cottage.
The mob pursued him inside, discovering a trembling child who whispered: Below.
Descending into the dark cellar vault, they uncovered the truth.
Chained to the damp stone walls were all the missing children—alive!
And dead upon the floor lay Tom Sutherland, the father of the very first missing girl.
Consumed by drunken madness, Sutherland had taken the children himself.
He was about to murder another captive when Herbert Solomon burst into the cellar, breaking the killer's neck to save the innocent.
The man they burned was their protector all along.
Centuries later, near the same woods, a little girl slipped into a raging river, swept toward jagged rocks.
From the forest bank, a tall, gaunt figure burst forth, plunging a pale, skeletal arm into the churning water to pull her to safety.
Even in death, Herbert Solomon was the kindest and gentlest of souls.
Would you have judged him by his face?
